utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, good afternoon to you. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Same goes for the Defence teams. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Nicholls. The accused is present -- sorry, the witness is present in the courtroom. There are some preliminary matters that we wish to raise, but we have decided first to go ahead with the testimony of the witness and try to finish it and then we will come to those matters afterwards. All right. Who is going first from the Defence teams? And you have all the time you require.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you proceed, witness and Mr. Mrkic, you both speak the same language. There is a tendency, it happens to us when we're speaking English, of course -- yes, in the meantime I am receiving interpretation of myself in French because I was on number 5, but I like to hear the French language. It is important that you allow a short pause between question and answer so as not to frustrate the work of our interpreters, which is already in itself extremely difficult. All right. Mr. Mrkic. Sorry for having interrupted you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday when you spoke about your education you said that you were an engineer. As far as I can understand your testimony, you didn't graduate from university?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I graduated from a high technical school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: A high technical school, very well. When did you finish that school?

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: And after that you served in the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: And did you find your first employment straight after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: When was that, when were you first employed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the spring of 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: So that means that you waited for a year to get your job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in 1984 I served in the army and in the -- 1985 I found a job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: What was your financial standing at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was of average financial means. My father was a worker, my mother was a housewife, and at -- an at-home mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Did you have any siblings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two sisters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Two sisters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkic, use your discretion as you go along as to when we need to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that most of my cross-examination will require private session, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Did you change employment quite often?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As was required every three or four years; relatively often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: When did you become politically active?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 90 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. The Court has rightly raised my attention to it. I would ask, I can't stop it rolling, to redact on page 2, I think, from -- after line 14 to page 3, line 6. As we're going,, I mean, I'm just afraid of the combination being put together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the time being at least we don't see a reason to redact those lines. If there is agreement of course between you and Mr. Mrkic that there will be other questions following, which, when answered, would give greater significance to these few lines, then of course we are -- would be prepared to redact. But we are not in a position -- we are not in Mr. Mrkic's mind, so we don't know. But for the time being I don't think we need to redact those lines. What's your position on that, Mr. Mrkic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the time being I don't think this is necessary. However, there will come a time when I will ask to go into private session and that will happen very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can go into private session immediately, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then let's go into private session and we don't need to redact what we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I would like to inform you that the Defence of Popovic, Miletic and Gvero won't have any questions for this witness, and the Defence of Nikolic said that they would need 45 minutes, but they will only use up 20 minutes. Therefore, we have decided to give our time to the Defence team of accused Beara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is new to me. I mean, you don't decide to give them time. I mean they have the time that we allow them to have. We are -- the fact that there are seven Defence teams doesn't mean that each one can ask for one hour or two hours and then give the one hour or two hours- to one of the other colleagues. That's -- that would be very bad court management, or case management on our part. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In part -- if I could just explain, in part, when we did the estimates several weeks ago and months ago when the witness initially appeared, that amount remained in our estimate. And I personally was the one who was putting the estimates in -- not in all, but in most of the cases. In this one I had recalled that I asked that it be increased from the initial hour to an hour 45, we were working under that presumption. And I believe I conveyed to the court clerk, and I am debating whether it is 100 per cent or not, so -- but that was my recollection of it. And I had asked the other defendants, accused, if they could assist us, just to put the Court at ease that we are not trying to prolong it. We are going directly to the issue here, and we know the Court's ruling prior that we cannot switch off, and, with all due respect, it was -- we're asking if we can do that so that there can be enough time to complete it within a reasonable period of time, and we know we are at your discretion on that issue, so that's why we're asking for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And reasonableness, Mr. Ostojic, should be the beacon, the guiding light for us all. We were informed now before we came in the courtroom that indeed you had asked for an hour 45 minutes. Which means that you haven't exhausted that time because Mr. Mrkic has been cross-examining the witness for a little bit less than an hour and a half. So we suggest that you try to, or he tries to finish the cross-examination within half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We did try, Your Honour, but in all honesty, as we try to be every day, it's hard to estimate sometimes the answer, question rapport, and we have indicated that we think we can finish it in an hour. We are not trying to prolong it. We're going right to the heart of the issue. Let's see how it goes, but I am advising the Court to be up-front with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed and then we will play it by the ear as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we will stop Mr. Mrkic if he doesn't go to the point. Our suggestion is that you try and focus on the -- the key issues in the testimony of this witness. Thank you. Mr. Mrkic. Mr. Mrkic, shall we go back to private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you. I don't think it will be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So, now, Witness, we are in open session. Please don't mention any details or names of persons or places that could identify you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I would like to focus on the statements you provided to the Prosecutor's office. My first question is about the meetings with the Office of the Prosecutor. Were you invited to these meetings, when was that, how did these meetings come about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got a telephone call from a -- an MUP employee of the MUP Zvornik and he told me when I was supposed to come to the police station in Zvornik for the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I suppose that he did not tell you what the topic of the interview would be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He just told me that I was invited to provide some information. It was just an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Were you told that you would appear at that meeting as a witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: What did you think at that time? Why do you think they were inviting you to that meeting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Did you suspect that they invited you because of you or because of somebody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: How did you feel during the interview? Did you have an impression that something was being requested from you, that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I have read that statement of yours. Could you agree with me if I said that the Prosecutor and his investigator asked you seven times before the break about the same topic, about your contacts with some officers from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure you will find it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember your answers to those questions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: What were your answers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I was not allowed to talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I have to correct you there. And if you don't agree with my correction, then we can look at the statement. Every time you said that you did not have any contacts with the officers from the Main Staff, only once you mentioned that you had a meeting with General Mladic. Every other time you your answer was negative. Every other time you said that you didn't have any contacts with the officers from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have some references to what he's talking about in the interview? It doesn't match my recollection. I'm not trying to take up time, I'd just like to know where specifically he's pointing to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. You have every right to raise this. Mr. Mrkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the interview that took place on the 7th of April, 2006, pages 12, lines --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the counsel could slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. The interpreters would like you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll start with the first page. Page 12, lines 12 through 14. Page 14, lines 10 through 12. To avoid any confusion, I'm talking about the B/C/S version of this interview. Page 14, lines 12 through 15. Again, page 14, lines 28 through 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: And this is your answer to the question about your meeting with General Mladic, in other words when you said that you did have a meeting with General Mladic. Page 16, lines 7 through 9.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I need to go on, I can do that, but I believe that the witness confirmed what I have just put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. This is what -- what I was going to say. First I was going to ask Mr. Nicholls whether he requires anything else. I think the references are there. Secondly, I would like the witness to repeat his answer, because it never made it to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what was the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: The question was are you aware what your answers were to each and every question that was relative to your contacts with the officers from the Main Staff? I'm paraphrasing those questions, I'm not quoting them. Your answer -- answer was always no, save for one answer when you said that you did have a contact or a meeting with General Mladic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, could I just clarify a point. Is what my friend is referring to when he said page 12, lines 12 to 14, the question which is on page 14 at line 4, "Okay, except Sreten Milosevic and this Mihajlo Galic, did you know any more officers from the Zvornik Brigade?" And then he says, "I knew the commander and I knew the deputy." Is that one of the questions he's saying was a question about the Main Staff, when he said he didn't know any? I'm just asking, for the record, for the references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's a fair question. Mr. Mrkic, since you are referring the witness to the Main Staff in particular, you need to clarify that to make sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 14, line 11 -- actually, 10. "Do you remember anybody from the Main Staff from those celebrations?" Answer on page 11, "Nobody from the Main Staff came." The same page, line 12, "Did you have any contacts with the officers from the Main Staff?" Line 13, "I remember -- I remember one contact. I was at a session of the Main Staff, General Mladic, Tolimir and Gvero came to that meeting that was attended by me and my 10 associates." On page 14, line 28, "Save for that one meeting did you have any other contacts with anybody else from the Main Staff?" Answer, "Yes, I did have a meeting, just one with General Mladic." Question, page 16, line 7, "After that meeting, did you meet any other officer from the Main Staff?" Answer is in line 9, and it reads, "No."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have covered them all. So let's go to the question. What's your question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let's go into private session for a short while. And pardon me saying this, but it's my tendency to be always on the cautious side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, I think I would like to go into private session for the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the presiding judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go back to private session. Thank you for -- and apologies to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify something which concerns yesterday's transcript. In one moment asked by the Prosecutor - if I'm wrong you may correct me - you answered that you were requested assistance to -- for the purpose of taking care of the prisoners. Is that correct? I believe this is a problem with translation, and this is why I wish to rectify and then clarify this. It is page 44, answer begins at line 19, and then goes over to line 1 on page 45. Do you recall saying, since I have the transcript in English, that it went for taking care and when -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that -- that prisoners had to be gotten rid of and he asked me assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Assistance in what? Assistance in what did he ask of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the burial, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Do you think, or are you certain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber appreciates that. The witness should know, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe the person that you spoke with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this was a briefing. It was not a dialogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Well, could you describe that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tall, camouflage uniform, well-built.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Colour of hair, colour of eyes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grey hair, age around 50, 55. That will be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please, let me rephrase my question. Do you recall when you sent -- saw Mr. Beara the next time when he was departing for The Hague? Did you express any doubts as to the identity of that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: When you expressed this to the OTP, what was their reaction to that? Did they show you some photographs to identify that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: This means you've come to a point where you are not certain or maybe you are not 100 per cent sure, however you would like to put it, that you saw this person on TV. This is what I forgot to ask you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: So you are not 100 per cent sure that that person was the person that you spoke to and --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the person on TV did not resemble the person who introduced himself as such and who held that briefing at the Zvornik Brigade barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Did the Prosecutor show you, although you have also said no, but did you try to identify in any way that person with whom you had spoken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They asked me about some details, whether he wore glasses, what he looked like and so on and so forth. I'm sure you will find it in the transcript of my interview. They asked me to describe him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: They didn't show you a photo of any kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: And now you are saying here as you sit here, that that person whom you saw on TV on the way to The Hague did not resemble the person with whom you had spoken previously?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mrkic. One moment. Yes, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. I have a few questions about your interview and your testimony today. (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we are back to square one. Yes, Mr. Nicholls. Shall we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So let's -- we can stay in open session. And redact lines 20 -- last part of line 23 on page 52 to lines 6 -- 7 of page 53. And if you are going ask him further questions on persons to whom he may have been related, or had contacts with at the time that could expose or will reveal his identity, then we will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, I believe you are right and that it would be advisable to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a short while and then revert back when it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Madam Nikolic has finished her cross-examination for accused Nikolic. Does anyone else wish to cross-examine the witness? Let's start with Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic or Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we don't have any questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, I think you have already made a statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the light of what's happened, I would be quite grateful if I could have a few minutes to discuss matters with my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And also, frankly, with my learned friend who prosecutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We understand that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Obviously in light of what was stated. So we will have the 25-minute break now. All right? And we will continue afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, I would like to know, however, before we go on break, Mr. Sarapa, will you be cross-examining this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for some half an hour, approximately. Not more than 45 minutes all together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Which should leave us time to deal with the so-called preliminaries which are now appendices. Yeah, okay. Let's have the 25-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am most grateful, Your Honour, and the Chamber will be relieved to here I have no cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. So that leaves us with Mr. Sarapa. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, any time you require us to go into private session, please, Mr. Sarapa, don't hesitate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For my first question, I will probably need to go into private session [as interpreted]. I will certainly have to go into private session for my third question, and for the later questions I will indicate to the Trial Chamber a time when private session is needed. I will probably not put such questions, but it is better to be in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, for your first question you need to go into private session. Let's go into private session straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not for the first two. Not for the first two questions. I will need private session for the third question. My two first questions are of a general nature and the answers cannot reveal the identity of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I was misled by the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Is it true that the units of the Territorial Defence in Zvornik municipality were organised on the principles of Leparskin [phoen], which means that there was no clearly-defined front-line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Is it true that the defence line would follow the form of concentric circles, depending on the prevalence of either the Muslim forces or the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-104 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now can we please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you provide for the redaction, please. And let's proceed. We never know what to expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that there are no further Defence teams that wish to cross-examine the witness. Is there re-examination, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we need to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Witness, that brings your testimony to an end, there being no further questions for you. Our staff will assist you, after you leave the courtroom. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony, and also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, before we proceed with the next witness, do you wish to tender any exhibits in relation to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. First, the pseudonym sheet under seal, P02457. And I would also tender, if there is no objection, the Zvornik Brigade duty officer logbook which I showed an excerpt to the witness. There are other witnesses who -- that will be discussed extensively in this trial, other witnesses will talk about it, but I would tender it now as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection? I hear none. So these two documents come in, are admitted. The first one of which is under seal. The second I don't think needs to under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It does not need to be. For a limited purpose, I would also tender the transcripts of the witness's interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It happens that sometimes we are telepathic, the members of the bench and we were all -- when I asked you whether this needs to be in -- under seal or not -- let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You asked if there are there was a question whether there were any objections and maybe we read in a bit too much. I just want to know if my colleague wants to enter just that one page he showed or if he wants entered the whole book. We believe it would be better to wait until we have another witness with the whole book, simply because this person is not a member of the Zvornik Brigade. This witness was not asked any questions what is the logbook, what its purpose is. That page we have no problem, but the rest we prefer to -- it comes with another witness who can explain that and also the dates because we will also have some questions concerning not only that logbook for that month, but the translation of the logbook for a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have made your point. What's your position after hearing Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine. I thought there might be something along those lines. We'll admit it later. It's been marked, we have the ID number for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think what Mr. Bourgon said makes sense. So we will only admit for the time being the pseudonym sheet under seal, and you are about to embark on a dangerous journey, so let's see how much wind is against you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's been dangerous for weeks, it feels like. The -- there was intensive cross-examination on this -- on these transcripts. Lots of propositions put to the witness, "you said this seven times," "you said this six times," and the references were given. I think that for Your Honours to evaluate as best you can the testimony of the witness on direct -- well not on direct, but on cross-examination, you're going to need that transcript to see whether he answered his -- whether the answers and the things put to him were correct or not. The second reason for putting it in is, there was a strong attack on the process in this case, the way the statement was taken, the way the Prosecution behaved in the statement, whether there was a record at all of this one portion of the interview. All that attack has been made and it's true that one question was withdrawn during the direct, during the cross-examination. But the allegations are still there, and I think it's important for Your Honours, since that strong attack was made, to see the entire record of what happened when, and how long. I cannot see even the possibility of prejudice in putting those statements in to you for the limited purpose, not for the truth of the matter, not as -- not as testimony, but simply to evaluate the testimony of the witness here, because if everything my learned friend said was correct, then it will -- that will be apparent, it will help you to get to the truth and to evaluate the testimony, if what I said was correct, the same. Maybe it will be in between. The Defence put portions of that statement on the screen, only the portions they wanted to. And I think you should be able to read the -- his interview in its entirety, to see whether it's true that he departed from his prior testimony, his prior statement, to see if it's true that he said that he had never had these meetings or that and this happened and to see if it's true that the Prosecution made no record of what occurred. I think it will help you with this important witness to be able to follow his testimony. Obviously it would not be given to a lay jury back home because they would not know how to assign the weight and purpose it was given to you, it is not particularly complex but it's not something they could do and it would be dangerous. But Your Honours know the only evidence you are going use is what the witness said before you here under oath, and you can use that to see whether or not the attacks on cross-examination were well-founded and whether the witness was correct in his answers, which were predicated on what he had said in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment on that, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, if I could address this. The two points raised by my learned friend on the basis for introducing such evidence do not honestly have any merit. First of all, the question with respect to the witness, whether he said that he was or was not, or had contact with the Main Staff on six, sevens occasions. I invited my learned friend that we could sit down at any time and go over it and we'll highlight specifically, and we gave him specific references to that. The witness, at the end of the day -- despite our attempt to highlight that, at the end of the day was asked the question and he answered it. He answered it, as I'm sure we all remember, without me telling the Court again what the answer is. So despite whether it was five, or seven, 10 times that we've stated -- that he denied having a meeting, he asked them, "Did you ever?", and he gave us that answer. So I don't believe that's a proper basis. The second basis, that there was an attack on the Prosecutor that my learned friend, co-counsel asked, it was withdrawn at the end of the day and he withdrew that question on the record, and we did apologise to him and we probably overstepped our bounds, our excitement in the courtroom, and we did apologise after the break. We withdrew the question. However, to cure that is not to put the statement in. To cure it would have been simply on redirect, which my friend had an opportunity to ask him specifically those questions on whether or not there was such involvement with the Prosecutor or prosecutorial misconduct. They didn't do that. Now they're trying through the back door to bring in a statement that covers more issues that they didn't cover in their direct, that we didn't cover in our cross, and I object to it and ask that the Court not allow this, even in this exception, but at any time to allow the Court to have these statements in, as you previously ruled. And I'm also just being given I am given a reference page, for the record as well, on page 33, lines 8 through 14, if the Court can look, during his testimony today, where what I just said was actually confirmed. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I took the opportunity at the last break to speak to Mr. Nicholls, and ask him what he intended to do. And he had the courtesy to tell me that he was going to make this application. Could I say two things: I -- we would much rather this interview was not admitted as an exhibit in this case. But secondly, and importantly, he has said in the last few moments to this Chamber that he's only asking for it to be admitted on a limited bases and not as to the truth of its contents. All I say before I sit down is, were the Chamber to admit it, and if so, we submit it should not be admitted. The Chamber should make it clear that it would only be admitted on that basis. And clearly the Chamber must consider Mr. Nicholls's application in relation to what he said and, in particular, the cross-examination that Mr. Mrkic embarked upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Are there any further -- yes, Mr. Bourgon. And then I will give you the floor again, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As a matter of principle, I fully support the positions taken by my colleague, Mr. Ostojic, and as well as my colleague, Mr. Josse. The idea is it's not for the Prosecution to ask to have the statement of a witness admitted into evidence. The only reason -- the only time where this should take place, if the Prosecution wants to use a statement after requesting permission and obtaining leave from the Court because they want to treat their own witness as a hostile witness. In some circumstances like this, it may happen that the Prosecution could ask for a statement to be admitted into evidence. But in this case, if somebody wants to decide what should go into evidence in terms of assessing the credibility of a witness, it has to be the Defence. In this case, the Defence of Mr. Beara is not requesting for that statement to go into evidence and that should be the end of the matter. If, as Mr. Ostojic said, in redirect questions had been asked with, again, leave to use the statement because it was used during the cross-examination, maybe again there could be established a -- Prosecution could establish a basis. But in this case, there is absolutely no basis for the Prosecution to ask for a witness statement to be admitted into evidence. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any further remarks? Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Nicholls? Please decide. And Madam Fauveau, if you wish to raise the same issue that you did yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to make a brief comment. We, as you know, will hear -- be hearing from many more witnesses of -- from the VRS and from the civilian Serb authorities that were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor. When the Defence challenges the integrity and absolute corruption, is the -- is what they accused us of, about turning off the tape, filling in answers. When they do that, they are putting the entire process of the interview in question. And I think our reputation and our performance here, we can deal with that. But if this is going to be an ongoing issue that we're going to have to listen to this each time, I think the door begins to get open on what really happened in that interview. I think that they have opened that door with what Mr. Meek said early on. And as I say, there's -- there's more at stake here than -- than merely the credibility of this witness and this particular interview, as I see this as a pattern where each important witness we have this big challenge to the integrity, either of the witness or of the Prosecution. As you will recall, this is happening over and over again. And I think there must be some logical consequences to this kind of conduct. As you saw, there was nothing to what Mr. Meek had said and the other questions were withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I made an argument, I didn't give evidence. And all I stated was that in this particular interview they violated their normal procedure, which is to not talk about the case when the tape recorder is turned off. You know, they never said I was wrong about that. You denied it and it's done. This is a backdoor way for them to try to get these statements in. I agree with Mr. Bourgon, in certain limited circumstances if they want to impeach their own witness, they can do that. Or in re-examination. They chose not to do either of those. So I don't believe that has any merit whatsoever. And frankly in all of these statements that I have seen in this case, this is the only time this happened. So, I mean, we're not saying this happens on a regular bases with the OTP. So in argument, certainly isn't evidence, I wasn't attacking them, I just said it was irregular. Big deal. Not a basis to let it in, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's confer. Any -- apart from this, any further documents that would you like to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey covered pretty much what I was going to say. Just very briefly, this is not novel. This has happened in other trials I've been in here, in the Limaj trial, and in other trials where document or witness statement is made of such extensive use it can be helpful for the Chamber to have it, and the Trial Chamber knows what weight to give it, which is none, other than adjusting, viewing the credibility of the witness. And I just have to disagree with Mr. Meek. I did deny what his allegations, it was not just sort of a friendly argument, it was a full frontal attack on what happened. And the only way I think to fix that is to put in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we are unanimous on this. Considering the extensive use that has been made of this -- these two interviews, we are of the opinion that we need them before us as a Trial Chamber, with the understanding - I need barely repeat that we are four professional judges that know exactly how to make use of these statements - but to be specific, as Mr. Josse himself suggested, they are being admitted to -- on a limited basis, as put by you, Mr. Nicholls. And certainly not for -- and not for the truth of -- of their contents. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sorry, neither our exhibit list nor the Prosecution's exhibit list was -- were both statements included. So I'm not sure, only the 7th of April 2006 was included. The 9th of April is not, and was not. So I don't -- we never relied on that statement in any of our questioning. The only questions came from the interview of the 7th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question for example was whether any of the two interviews, whether it was true that in both interviews he never mentioned Colonel Beara, for example. That was one question. How -- how --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How can we come to a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honour, I wouldn't want to debate that with you and it's your recollection. But I am certain that that was not raised because the second interview had something totally different to do than the first interview. So I'm confident we didn't raise it in that manner, but I will take a look at it and ask the Court to merely reserve it so that we can re-address that issue tomorrow. And I will closely go through the transcript to look at that again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have these two transcripts admitted. I don't know the dates. You need to tell us the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Over our objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Judge, just for the record. I apologise, excuse me. Just for the record, look at page 71, starting at line 16 when Mr. Nicholls makes his argument. He says that in other trials where a witness's statement is made, and he made that earlier, "statement." He didn't come around to "statement" until later in his argument because he knows that we never -- no one made any cross-examination to do with the second statement. It was all about the first statement. And Mr. Nicholls knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's not true. I said "statement" as a generic term. That means statement, this is his statement, it is one statement. The second statement is putting on the record what was said during the first statement. It is one statement and it was made use of, as Your Honour picked up. It was this, you have never said this, you never said that. This was in the included, and I think the Court has made its ruling. And if that statement is not of value, then it is a nullity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Listen, I am not used, after having handed down a decision, to reopen the discussion unless there is -- is something, but for that matter you have referred us to page 71, I can refer you to page 66, line 3, where he is definitely referring to transcripts and not transcript. But anyway, the discussion on this is closed. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We will be asking for certification of this decision in order to go before the Appeals Chamber. We believe that this is an issue that does go and we will do that in writing, Mr. President. And I would also ask that we ask for a stay of the Trial Chamber's decision until we get decision on both certification, and the case may be before the Appeals Chamber. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is -- but we will deal with both. In the meantime, they are admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then we will await your motion for certification.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we will join that, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will join that, obviously, as well just so the Court -- when he said "we," I was assuming he was going to just --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, if you could avoid overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You mean you want to join in as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, Judge, I want to correct what I said earlier. Page 66, line 10, where Mr. Nicholls is asking and speaking about what's correct and not, the second reason for putting it in, "there was a strong attack on the process in this case, the way the statement was taken." And he knows it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I sent my message loud and clear when the decision has been taken. No further discussions, please. One thing that we need to clear up, because there may have been a small misunderstanding. That Zvornik Brigade duty officer logbook, you have withdrawn that, you are not tendering at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, not at this time. We will do that later with another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So -- yes. Now, we come to documents from the Defence. Beara team.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may again handle this. Just to go quickly, we would like to tender 2D64, 7D238, 2D67, and 2D68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections on the part of the Prosecution? Or for that matter from any of the Defence teams because they may have an interest too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't think they put 2D64 and 67 to the witness. But I don't have any strong objection to that. They talked about it. I don't see the need for 2D68 to come in, but I -- I guess I don't have any really strong objection to it. It -- the -- I just don't see the need for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to respond to that, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The Court should grant my request since they don't have any other objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to tell Mr. Nicholls, when in doubt -- the rule is when in doubt, don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In all seriousness, with respect to 2D68, a lot was covered. I think the Court will look through that document because it's an OTP witness in another case who specifically highlights certain aspects of what we consider to be crimes that may have been committed or were committed, at least alleged by this witness, by the witness that we've just heard. And I think you can see the two points that he differentiates between certain witnesses that he claims were perpetrators of those crimes. So we think it is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it you are not submitting this for the truth of its contents either.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We hope to bring the witness forward on that, with the assistance of the Prosecutor, so we can locate him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkic is looking for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, any objections from any of the Defence teams? None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The conclusion we arrive at or two, I don't know, which is the right one, is that these four documents are all being admitted, and they will be marked accordingly by our staff. Or by the Registrar. Does anyone else, Mr. Sarapa or Madam Nikolic, do you wish to tender any documents? Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. So that comes to an end. Now, yesterday we adjourned with some unfinished symphonies still ongoing. One was declaration from you, Mr. McCloskey, that following the statement by Mr. Vanderpuye you had given instructions for a thorough check and recheck of the documentation that may relate to Ms. Frease's testimony. And that depending on that first you would give us information on that and secondly depending on that we would know more or less when to expect her to return. So can you update the Trial Chamber on that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I believe Mr. Vanderpuye has the -- has the latest on that, and I hope it's good news.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So in that case, you needn't hide behind the column, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Please excuse my positioning this afternoon. Good afternoon to you, Mr. President, to Your Honours, counsel. I do have the latest on that, and the latest on that was that we had completed a search of all of the data archives of -- in our database. And we did identify some additional documents which I furnished to the Defence late last evening, I think around -- close to 10.00. That's about the time that we got through sorting through what we found, and turning over what we thought we were responsible to turn over. I don't know if the Defence has had an opportunity to go through those documents, digest them and prepare themselves for cross-examination. But I'm informed by the investigation team that undertook this search and others that we have completed a thorough search of our database. I also did check to see if there were any physical files lying around in the area where Ms. Frease previously worked, and there were no such files. I also asked the investigator to check if there were cupboards or cabinets or things of that nature to identify if there were any such files and I am told that there were none. What we have turned over I think represents the totality of the documents relevant to Ms. Frease's testimony that we don't believe are covered by Rule 70, paragraph A, as we discussed yesterday. That's the news. She's here, and we're prepared to proceed. I believe -- I believe the Defence is aware that she's here today because I think you had invited her to come back to be cross-examined today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, does any one of the Defence team wish to address the Trial Chamber? Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we received the documents yesterday regarding General Miletic we can continue with the cross-examination of Ms. Frease, but before doing so I'd like to raise a question. Among the documents we received yesterday there are five reports, informative reports taken by the Prosecutor during interviews with witness who have already testified. PW-131, PW-129, PW-124, PW-136, and PW-145. These documents have been in the possession of the OTP since 1999 because that's the time when the reports were drafted. Yesterday I raised the issue of an apparent breach of the Rule 68 obligation by the Prosecutor. I spoke to the Prosecutor about it. We never agree on this. What we think is Rule 68 obligation is not considered so by the Prosecutor. I can understand why information can be understood differently by both sides, but here we are in a case of violation of Rule 66(A)(ii) and there is no possibility of a dual interpretation of the -- such rule. The Defence was not able to duly prepare for cross-examination. I'm not in a position to tell you whether the cross-examination would have been any different, but I'm very worried. We have received today information statements, basically, by witnesses who have already testified in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment on that, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's my understanding that there -- that's correct, though the -- Ms. Frease was at interviews with investigator Dean Manning, and Dean Manning's statement of that, of that witness, has been provided to the Defence. Ms. Frease in a few situations had made an additional note or two about something the person had said and those, when we found them, we turned them over. I didn't find anything particularly significant in -- in any of those additional bits, but when we found them, yes, we should have turned them over and -- but I don't see any -- any -- any Rule 68 in them. But we of course remain available to bring back someone, if -- if there's some need or we can -- but I frankly don't see anything that gets anywhere near that. But we are -- we're -- we wanted to make this as correct as we possibly can. But these are small details that Ms. Frease added in addition to the statement that the person had. I believe that's -- that's correct, and Mr. Vanderpuye agrees with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think what I can say is that, strictly speaking, we are seized of a submission but not of a specific request, so I won't say anything more on it. Later on, if we are at any time seized with the issue that you raised, Madam Fauveau, we'll give opportunity to the Prosecution, to yourself, to air your views and then we'll hand down a decision. And that applies of course not just to you, but any -- because we're talking of witnesses that testified in the trial. Mr. Haynes, yesterday, towards the end of the session, of the sitting, raised an issue relating to a motion of yours, Mr. McCloskey, to convert 12 witnesses to 92 ter witnesses. And my impression, after having heard both of you, was that maybe you could have a roundtable between you, amongst you and in regard to one or two of these witnesses you could make one kind of submission in relation to others, maybe another. Have -- what I want to know is two things: Whether you have met and discussed this, and whether you have come to some kind of agreement amongst you or between you, and then, depending on the answer, I will move to my next question. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have had a chance to talk about it briefly. He's given me the names of two of the three people I think that he was interested in. He made sense, and I want to go back and take a look at those witnesses. It may be simpler for everyone to just do a brief direct on some of them. But I need more hours in the day, unfortunately, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I mean ... Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just to fill you in, of the original 12, I considered that the application is perfectly good in relation to eight of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Without --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you tell me straight and plain whether there is agreement to convert the testimony of Mr. Peccerelli?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When is that witness due to come over? Because I thought I was going to expect him after witness PW-104.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He is in my office right now, but we're hoping to get Ms. Frease done first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have, as you know been discussing amongst ourselves on all this, and Judge Kwon would like to say -- state something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't it will affect, at the end of the day, the actual conduct of the examination, but my question was whether we need 92 ter at all in case of expert witnesses. With the regime, that kind of regime or format of examination has been possible, even before the existence of 92 ter, so can I hear your observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At this point I'm confused with 92 ter and 92 bis and 94 and A and B and -- but most of our experts are 92 bis and the plan is a very -- well, 15 minutes, maybe 30 minutes, there is some new issues that have arisen that you may want to hear about, but yes, I don't know if we need to do 92 ter for experts. Most of them have already been 92 bis, and I think that kind of covers -- covers the issue that we are all concerned about. But if there is something in particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then there comes another tukwej [phoen] issue between the relationship between 92 bis and 94 bis. But as long as there is agreement between the parties, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. I don't think I will add anything to what Judge Kwon said. In reality, these, Peccerelli and someone else, I forgot his name now -- yes, Dakwija [phoen], were two experts that you wanted to bring forward to testify viva voce. They were not included in the 92 ter list. So I think you can understand Judge Kwon's statement, even better, after having said that. Gentlemen, and ladies, before then, shall we come -- recommence with Ms. Frease? Is there any objection? None. Shall we bring her in, please. We are not going finish with her today, obviously, I mean, but we will make a serious attempt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just a housekeeping -- she can come in, fine. I am informed that -- with one of these, that Mr. Baraybar is here, is from Peru. He's here to testify in the -- what we call the MOS case, the Kosovo case. He was -- the Prosecution cannot seem in that case to figure out when he's going to testify. We're actually -- they're doing -- trying to do the same thing we are, and we'll try to -- as soon as we can sort out when he will be able to testify in both these cases, we will inform you. But I am told that he cannot testify on Monday. That may be because he's in the MOS case and we don't want him to be on the witness stand in two cases at the same time, if we can help it. Anyway that's a detail, we will inform everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will go down in history if we succeed in doing that. Have him in two witness boxes at the same time. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We finally made it, Ms. Frease. And you will be here for less than 15 minutes, that's more or less the time left. But we will proceed today and then we will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who wishes to go next? Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Judge. I have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't promise you an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Is it possible at all to see a document that Mr. Zivanovic presented to me when I was here last?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you tell us which document it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the fuel order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Do you need to see it today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or can you see it tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will be brought tomorrow and shown to you. Unless you need to see it today in the wake of any question that may be put.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will do that. Mr. Ostojic, again my apologies to you for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, again, Ms. Frease. Or good evening again. The last time we met a couple days ago, I put a question to you and then we ended basically for the day. Do you remember the question?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I asked you that you have used the word during your testimony in this case, "independently corroborated," and in other testimonies you have used "internal consistency" to establish that corroboration. Did those two words, "independently corroborated" and "internal consistency," mean the same thing to you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be depend on the context, but I would say not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And describe for me how it wouldn't?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it possible for you to give me examples of cases where I've used those two terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You have in the Krstic case, for example, in looking at certain intercepts you said to Judge Wald, I believe, that these documents show an internal consistency, and that that was an - I am summarising for you. I could get it for you exactly - that that was the basis for you showing that they were corroborative with each other.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that example I would say that I was -- hold on just a second. Let me read your question again. That -- that I was probably referring to material contained within the intercepts. And the subject matter within the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You shared with us in your intercept binder a sample, as you called it, of the intercepts you showed, there was some corroboration. Did you find in any of the intercepts independent corroboration as opposed to corroboration with other intercepts from other logbooks like I think you did for an intercept that was purportedly captured on the 14th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which intercept on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The one that you testified about involving, purportedly, Mr. Beara and General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In the binder you show that there is four entries in four different sources. My question is just -- to put it right to you, other than those intercepts which are internally consistent, according to you, did you have any other independent corroboration with respect to that intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was an intercept on the 15th of July. The one -- you're speaking about the one at 9.55, 9.57, and 10.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the binder is right in front of you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is. There is another conversation that relates to those three from the 13th of July at 1919, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You said that, but I'm talking about independent from the logbooks themselves, or the printouts, was there --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could we avoid overlap, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Other than the notebooks themselves, and the printouts as you've testified to, was there any other independent source of corroboration?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us, Ms. Frease, your efforts to obtain third party or independent sources in -- that you utilised in the determining whether or not the logbooks were authentic?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think we've talked about this before, right. Using videotape, using notes from UNPROFOR, note-takers of conversations between UN officials and members of the VRS. A lot of VRS documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you find that third party independent source, even though it includes one of the participants or parties, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, what about independent, as I call them, third party sources, like you mentioned in your testimony the other day on page 44, lines 9 through 11, and again on page 31, line 5, that you mentioned, and I will -- I think I'm quoting it directly, but you were asked by my learned friend, Mr. Zivanovic, did you double-check it in any way, and you gave an answer, and then you said, "not with an outside handwriting expert." So I want to talk about that a little bit, and using this outside handwriting expert, do you think he would qualify as a third party, independent source?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're talking about when the notebooks -- let -- let me preface it by saying I don't know precisely what the skills of a -- a -- of a handwriting expert or an expert in ink and dating ink and all of that, what they are able to do, what they're able to determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, did you inquire ever?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you inquire if a handwriting expert can determine the age of a piece of paper, that he can tell you exactly when that paper was manufactured?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you inquire of any third party, independent source, including a forensic handwriting expert, to determine whether the logbooks were manufactured or put in the market on a certain given date?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Who is Mr. Ten Camp?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten Camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think. Or is it Kemp? Camp? He is a forensic handwriting expert that the Office of the Prosecution used from time to time in other cases. Have you ever used the handwriting expert to determine the authenticity of the logbooks that we are discussing in this case?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever call the manufacturer of the logbooks to determine when the logbooks were actually created?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did anyone under your direction when you took over this intercept project, as we've called it from time to time?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the year of the publication of these logbook or notebooks are?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do see that the question has been answered. The objection is -- I do see that the question has been answered but the objection is I would ask my learned friend to put a more specific question to the witness since it is not clear that all the logbooks were manufacturing or not at a given date or time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's very fair, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I mean, Ms. Frease, very quickly this way: You have no idea, in fact, that -- when any of the notebooks were manufactured, meaning you don't know if they were manufactured all at the same time or they were manufactured over a period of time, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, did you ever notice in any notebook that there was bar-code information on one of the logbooks or some of the logbooks?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I paid specific attention to bar-codes, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with what a bar-code is? We see it every day in a grocery store when they have us zip through the lines, right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What do you think is contained in those bar-code information sheets that are on things such as logbooks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That question clearly calls for speculation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought, if she knows. I know what a bar-code contains, for example, so ... Yes, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's her answer to you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you could summarise for us briefly, the printouts for a second, do you know if the information that was above the line, the prefatory information, whether or not that was placed in the computer and generated by the computer automatically, or were intercept operators able to input dates or other significant information on that portion of the printouts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will have to make an assumption here. Because I had left at the time that the electronic copies were decoded and electronically stamped by the evidence unit here. In looking at the electronic copies and seeing that a couple of the dates were incorrectly typed, I would assume that they had the ability to type the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now -- and I know we only have a couple of minutes. I'm just trying to understand, when you were the lead person or head person of this intercept project, you had many people working for you. Did you record when you had meetings with these people? Like a memo to file?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You assume I had many people working. I think that's an assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise for that, but I thought your testimony was, just to try to short circuit it, that you had translators working for you, investigators working for you, researchers working for it, and it's my mistake probably but whatever the number of people were, did you maintain a record of meetings with those people?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. When you met with witnesses, did you also create or generate what's known as an information sheet or an information report?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When would you and when wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would create -- for example, I would create an information report if I met with someone and perhaps didn't take a statement from them, but we had a conversation in which they provided information that -- that was important, that was relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you would be the sole determining person -- or you would be the sole person to determine whether that information was important or relevant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes it was very easy to know whether the information was relevant or not. If I ever had a question about anything, I always asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How many intercept operators did you personally interview?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a specific number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: More or less than 10?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say less.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll go over them. Hopefully tomorrow. While interviewing these intercept operators, did you recognise or find that there were some inconsistencies between their stories?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "their stories"?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: By how they told you they were required to fill in the logbook, when they received the logbook, whether or not they knew the participants in the logbook, whether changes should be made to the logbook, when changes or modifications should be entered into the logbook, things of that sort.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't inconsistencies with respect to -- as far as I remember, with respect to when they needed to fill in the logbook, because all of the conversations recorded by the military at that time, during the time period that we're talking about, there was a requirement to record the conversations in logbooks. When they received logbooks there might have --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It might be our time. Her microphone is flashing, I think, and that's why she's hesitating. Someone's sending her a signal from somewhere, with all due respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It may mean it's 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think let's adjourn here, and your question was extensive in any case, so I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It was just to put her in the context and I'm going break it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's a fair question. And I think it needs to be broken down into the various -- and then she will respond to it tomorrow. Tomorrow we are sitting in the morning and not in the afternoon --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- so we will meet here at 9.00 in the morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 2nd day of March, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
